html:
The family of Iron Age peoples across central and western Europe who spoke Celtic languages, from about 800 BCE until Rome conquered most of them in the 1st century BCE. They were never one nation. Archaeologists trace them through two cultures named after sites in Austria and Switzerland.

Hallstatt (about 800 to 450 BCE), named after a salt-mining village in Austria. Chiefs grew rich on salt, iron and trade with the Greeks and Etruscans, and were buried with wagons, gold and Greek wine vessels.

La Tène (about 450 BCE to the Roman conquest), named after a site on Lake Neuchâtel. It is known for its art of swirling curves on metalwork. In this phase Celtic groups spread widely:

  • Gauls sacked Rome in about 387 BCE.
  • Others attacked Delphi in 279 BCE, and some crossed into Anatolia, where they became the Galatians.
  • Celtiberians lived in Spain, and Britons and Gaels in Britain and Ireland.

Late Celtic Europe had large fortified towns, the oppida, coins and long-distance trade. Druids, a learned priestly class, kept laws and lore by memory, since writing was little used.

The end came from Rome. The Romans took northern Italy and southern Gaul, and Julius Caesar conquered the rest of Gaul from 58 to 50 BCE, beating Vercingetorix at the siege of Alesia in 52 BCE. Celtic languages survived in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, where Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Breton are still spoken.
